Copper Quarterly Report October 2009 

# Executive Preview 

## On the cusp 



- This note updates CRU’s analysis of the copper market outlook in advance of LME Week. We will issue our final forecast later in October, taking on board any new developments and issues that may come to light during our conversations and discussions with clients and industry participants over the week. 



- The copper market, along with many other commodities, paused for breath in Q3 2009 and the question now is: Where to from here?  CRU believes that the converging factors of scrap replacement, restocking and demand recovery in China are not likely to re-emerge over the remainder of the year.  Moreover, with the SHFE-LME arbitrage window closed, Chinese refined imports will be capped. 



- China will continue to see strong growth in consumption in 2010.  Restocking-led growth in the world ex-China will boost demand in H1, as well, and we foresee a modest deficit and higher prices.  We anticipate demand growth will ease back in H2 2010 as restocking ends in the world ex-China.  At the same time, with prices above production costs at all but the most expensive mines, refined output is expected to ramp-up through the year to register growth of 3.4% next year.  With most of this growth in the second half of the year, coupled with anaemic demand, the market is expected to shift into surplus and prices should fall back. 



- Prices are forecast to remain above the mine cost curve in 2011, and with a slower year for demand growth we expect another annual surplus and a build up of reported inventory above 1.6Mt, forcing prices lower.  Another round of mine cutbacks is likely, as a result of the lower prices, and the market should move back into deficit from 2012.  However, a stock overhang should prevent prices from rising significantly above $5,700/t over 2013-2014. 

The recent supply disruption at Batu Hijau and now at Olympic Dam, alongside the threat of a strike at Spence may well influence sentiment and see copper prices spike higher in the short-term, despite lacklustre underlying demand growth.

ternational Limited confidential 2 Copper Quarterly Report October 2009 Executive Preview ### Chinese divergence Copper prices have more than doubled this year despite our estimate of a significant surplus in the global market. However, rather than the global level, it is the reaction in the world ex-China to developments in China that have driven the copper price so far this year. The market exChina saw a shift from surplus into deficit in the first half due to the high level of Chinese refined imports. This shift into deficit reflects developments in China specifically, which we believe will drive consumption growth in the country of 15% in 2009. - **Scrap replacement** : Chinese scrap imports fell earlier this year due to lower scrap generation in the main industrialised markets and the reluctance of scrap traders to sell into China following defaults in Q4 2008. - **Restocking** : following excessive destocking in Q4 2008 Chinese semis producers restocked. This was further exaggerated by their decision to replace scrap with cathode. - **Stocking** : several large new rod mills that use refined cathode as feed have started up in 2009. These mills required working stocks which boosted refined imports, highlighting ongoing semis import replacement. - **Underlying demand recovery** : the Chinese government’s stimulus measures boosted underlying demand after the Chinese New Year in February, and demand has stayed reasonably strong thereafter. - **Speculation** : speculative buying in China was inadvertently fuelled by the loose monetary policy that is a key part of the government’s stimulus plan. ### 2009 price movements better reflect Chinese developments than those at global level LME cash price and supply/demand balance*, quarterly, 2006-2009

However, the lag between booking and the arrival of material meant that Chinese imports of refined copper hit a new all-time high in June and remained at almost 300,000t in July. At the same time, the recession in the industrialised world seemed to have hit bottom in Q3. It would appear that investors in the industrialised world took this as a signal to buy into asset classes, such as copper, that would benefit from the economic recovery. Barclays Capital estimates that commodity assets under management on behalf of institutional and retail investors increased by 19% q-on-q in Q2. These investment flows helped support prices around the $6,000/t level, as fresh Chinese buying eased back. There are still concerns over demand in the short term, with refined copper consumption in the world outside of China set to slump by 17% this year. We have not seen the seasonal upturn in demand that usually occurs in September in the mature industrialised countries. At the same time, there was less of a seasonal downturn in China, due mainly to a rebound in copper tube demand following the success of the government’s incentive schemes for consumers to purchase domestic appliances. However, this leads us to the conclusion that demand in China is not likely to accelerate much in Q4. Moreover, the latest Chinese trade data for August indicated a further decline in refined imports. We believe that there is sufficient capacity to consume any excess inventory that may well have built up in China. Our estimates are closer to 500,000t rather than the rumoured 1.2Mt. In addition, easing scrap availability will also dampen the requirement for imports of refined cathode over the reminder of this year. ### …while World ref

ined output falls, but only by 4.5%… Mine production has continued to surprise on the upside so far this year. However, over the next few months several labour agreements will be negotiated. The risk of strikes if negotiations fail lies mainly in Chile, where most labour contracts will be negotiated by the end of 2009, including at Escondida and Chuquicamata, which between them produced 1.625Mt of copper in 2008 (10% of world copper mine production in 2008). CRU International Limited confidential 4 Copper Quarterly Report October 2009 Executive Preview Earlier this year, labour contract negotiations at Lomas Bayas led to an 8-day strike and a 4% pay increase, and other benefits. Currently union workers at Chile's Spence copper mine are considering an improved offer from BHP Billiton. If workers reject this offer there is a strong likelihood of strike action. The Spence negotiations are likely to set a precedent for the rest of the labour discussions (Escondida and Chuquicamata) that are due late in 2009. However, if disruptions occur due to strikes they are more likely to affect mine production next year. Although smelter cutbacks provided some relief to the concentrate market, copper concentrate supply will still fall well short of demand, especially as Chinese smelters try to maximise their output to support domestic cathode demand. ### …leaving prices vulnerable to a decline in Q4 this year Prices have defied the global fundamentals so far this year. In the first half of the year the market will be broadly balanced as restocking driven growth on the back of improving macro economic sentiment and seasonally higher H1 demand in China will see demand growth outstrip that of production. This will support higher prices, as will the potential of strikes at miners in Latin America. Anaemic demand and stronger supply growth through the second half of the year will see the market revert back to surplus. This should lead to higher inventories and we expect prices on the LME to fall back by year end. ### Production pressures still remain In 2011-2014, global demand is forecast to grow by 5.1% per annum, led by China. Over this period, mine production is set to expand by over 1Mt. Five South American concentrate projects (Salobo, Toromocho, Esperanza, Los Bronces and Alejandro Hales (Mansa Mina)) will be responsible for much of this increase. Meanwhile, increasing smelting capacity, mostly in China, will exacerbate the persistent imbalance between concentrate production and demand. Refined production should grow by xxx% in 2011. 2011 will be the fourth consecutive year of surplus and will see inventory build to over 1.6Mt. We would anticipate that this will lead to lower prices which will trigger production cutbacks at the mines throughout 2012. This would see the market shift back into a modest deficit. Even though the market remains in deficit, a stock overhang should prevent prices from rising significantly above $5700/t in 2013 and 2014. ### Points to watch #### **Downside** - The main downside threat is from a double-dip recession. The financial sector in the industrialised world is still fragile, with further consumer spending constrained and debt repayment threatening more loan defaults and pressure on bank balance sheets. - China could also overheat, resulting in inflation and monetary tightening. - Investors could see more potential upside in the global manufacturing sector during a new upswing. If copper looks less attractive relative to other alternatives, they could become net sellers. - Economisation and substitution: Will the record gap between copper prices and those of competing materials (especially aluminium) go away, or lead to a return of the substitution threat? - There are some unknowns that make it difficult to reconcile imports vs. stock-building in China. We see these as part

of the obscurity associated with the Chinese statistics and the stock build in China could be higher or lower than we estimate. 



- Automotive: scrappage schemes have only brought forward demand from future quarters threatening another mini-boom/bust cycle in 2010 as schemes are unwound. 



- Construction: Lack of credit growth threatens an extended period of weak growth.

#### **Upside** 



- The industrialised world could see a quicker economic recovery than forecast, which would see more rapid re-stocking and a jump in the price. 



- Mine underperformance will generally provide support for prices.  Strikes in South America could boost the price in the short run.  Beyond 2010, a return of production growth threatens a return of high capital cost inflation (as during the boom years), as miners scramble to obtain equipment to expand operations. 



- Should prices fall as forecast, we anticipate the SRB would come back into the market to continue replenishing stocks, which could spark another round of speculative buying. 



- There is upside price potential if investors choose to view copper as a long-term asset class play.  However, with equity markets improving and the fact that commodity indices have not been able to gather any additional upward momentum over the past two months, the potential to earn higher returns in commodities in Q4 2009 and Q1 2010 may have run its course. 

This report is based on information available up to 6<sup>th</sup> October 2009.
